The Mandela R5 myth

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A Mandela R5 coin recently sold for R2.5 million, but experts say the actual value is no more than R5. CB investigates

Summary:
We have been approached by several case studies who have complained about a coin dealership known as SA Coin. Our case studies all say they've been scammed by SA Coin, who made promises of lucrative returns on R5 Mandela coins which are supposedly very valuable to coin collectors. The R5's are punted as investments, with up to 200% returns offered and SA coin also promise to buy back the coins after 5 years if the investors can't get them sold. This, according to our case studies is not the reality. SA Coin are not making good on their promises to buy back the coins, and our case studies can't sell them for more than their actual value of R5.

Further information:
One of our case studies has spent R75000 on a single coin, but it now has no value as a collectible. Other coins, which are still being sold for anything between R3500 - R100000, don't have any value either. According to Glen Schoeman Chairman of the SA Association of Numismatic Dealers, several coin sellers are creating a false market for these coins, which really have no collectible or monetary value other than R5.Our hiddencam footage shows just how persuasive the SA Coin pitch is, and also how they make promises they won't be able to keep and never put on paper. We have also asked two of our case studies to phone SA Coin and offer their coins for sale at 10% of the value they were bought from SA Coin for. Ofcourse
SA Coin will not buy these back. We are also able to prove through grading reports from the only 3 internationally accepted coin grading agencies that the Mandela coins are not rare and never will be. Documentation from the SA Mint shows that millions of Mandela R5 coins were minted and are in circulation - no matter how high a grade a Mandela coin receives, it will never be seen as a rare coin.

Press Release:


Mandela R5 Myth
A Mandela R5 coin recently sold for R2.5-million, but experts say the actual value is no more than R5. In fact, the majority of so-called Mandela coins are worth nothing more than R5. But several eager investors have lost thousands on commemorative coins, with false promises of returns of up to 200%. Are coin dealers creating a false market for coins with no value other than their actual denomination? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


R5 Mandela Myth
1st Draft Script
07 Oct 2015

Voice
Coin collecting dates back to Roman times, where coins were often hoarded for their bullion value. It remains a popular and lucrative hobby today – this South African 1902 Veldpond for example, in mint condition, could be worth in excess of R500 000.

Link Claire
Investing in coins has always been an exclusive yet difficult club to break into – until the mid 2000’s when coin dealers jumped on the bandwagon and started promoting the Mandela R5 coin as the next big investment opportunity – promising massive returns on investment. But have investors seen those returns?

Voice
We’ve received numerous complaints from viewers who feel they’ve been duped into investing in Mandela R5 coins – a series of coins minted by the South African Mint commemorating former president Nelson Mandela’s 90th Birthday, his presidency and his inauguration. Our viewers are all pointing fingers at this company, SA Coin and it’s CEO Mark Anderson.

Sound Up Cyprian Richards
He’s grossly inflated the prices…

Voice
Cyprian Richards says he bought three Proof grade R5 Mandela coins from SA Coin for R1.125 million – an amount that made up a sizable piece of his retirement funds. According to him both the broker and SA Coin CEO Mark Anderson assured him that the coins would double in value in a matter of months or they would refund him his original purchase price.

Sound Up Cyprian
He said then if you’re not happy, if it doesn’t materialize, in other words if these coins don’t double the way I say they would, you can bring them back in January and we’ll refund your money. And that never ever happened.

Voice
Husband and wife Stephan and Michelle Kapp were looking for a good investment opportunity when they read about the R5 Mandela coins on SA Coin’s website.

Sound Up Stephan & Michelle
Stephan: We looked on the Internet, typed in investment opportunities, and came about SA Coin’s website. And we read staggering reviews and numbers that you cannot imagine.

Voice
SA Coin’s newsletter The Coin Report was predicting that Proof 70 Mandela Birthday R5 coins would be selling at R500 000 by the end of 2012 and at R1 million by the end of 2013. The same publication also flaunted a 2008 90th birthday R5 Mandela Coin that SA Coin claimed to have sold for R2.5 Million rand. Impressed with the figures, the Kapps were convinced that it was a good deal and bought a Proof 69 Mandela R5 coin.

Sound Up Michelle
And they actually said to us that we must actually buy it as quickly as possible because it is such a fast appreciating coin that that same coin will be R85 000 by the end of that month. So we paid R75 000 for our coin.

Voice
Barry Hutton bought five MS66 Mandela R5 coins from SA Coin for R9 500 in 2009.

Sound Up Barry Hutton
The broker that sold it to me, he basically stated that I can cancel all my retirement annuities, the returns on this were astronomical, I obviously didn’t do that, thank goodness, but they said it’s the fastest growing investment in the world.

Voice
None of our case studies have been able to sell their coins for anywhere near what they paid for them – but Cyprian has lost the most.

Sound Up Cyprian
… I contacted all the coin dealers… they all knew that I’d been scammed, and they said: “no way’s that’s probably worth R10 000” the one coin and the other was worth R15 000. So something that was paid for a million, they were prepared to offer R25 000. And that’s it.

Voice
That means Cyprian’s investment is currently only worth 2.22 percent of what he originally paid for it – a far cry from the kinds of growth predicted by SA Coin on their website….

Link Claire
So if Mandela coins are as valuable as advertised, surely discerning coin collectors wouldn’t hesitate at an opportunity to add them to their collection.

Sound Up Eelco
I have not met one discerning coin collector, and when we say discerning coin collector we’re talking about people who’ve made this a passion, I would say there’s not one discerning coin collector who’s invested in these R5 Mandelas that I know of.

Voice
Eelco Lodewijks is a former coin dealer and passionate coin collector. He says some dealers are charging exorbitant amounts for Mandela R5 coins.

Sound Up Eelco
Claire: Are those realistic estimates or values attached to those R5 coins?

Eelco: … somebody had said they had sold one for a R100 000, and I was selling them in my shop for R200 in a cd case…

Voice
Determining the value of a coin is a complicated business, but two key factors are the scarcity and condition of a specific specimen. The condition is determined through the internationally accepted Sheldon scale – a grading system that determines the state of a coin from 0 – being the lowest, to 70, which basically means the coin, is flawless.

Sound Up Glenn
In South Africa the R5 coin has been a bit of a problem.

Voice
Glenn Schoeman is the chairman of the South African Association of Numismatic dealers, a non-profit organization of professional numismatists, or people who study coins.

Sound Up Glenn Schoeman
Claire: Looking at the history of the R5 coin though, especially the Mandela R5 coin, has anyone made a substantial profit in investing in those coins?

Glenn: I don’t know anybody who has actually made a big profit out of R5 coins, I know of a couple of dealers who might have, but I don’t know of any investors as such who have actually made any big money out of R5 coins.

Voice
Since the only returns investors we spoke to have made to date have been substantial losses, we decided to speak to SA Coin CEO Mark Anderson, who says they can’t be blamed for the poor performance of the Mandela coin investments.

Sound Up Mark
Claire: What would you say to those people who feel like they’ve been hard done by?

Mark: So we give our prognosis on where we feel the coins will go in the future and if the coins don’t perform due to tight economic conditions there’s nothing we can do about it.

Voice
SA Coin brokers never mentioned tight economic conditions to our case studies though. Instead, the coins were punted as the investment opportunity of a lifetime.

Sound Up Barry
Claire: Did he give you any specific figures on how that investment would grow per annum?

Barry: Well they basically stated that they would double in value year on year, and within a few years it would be worth about twenty times what I was purchasing at that point in time.

Sound Up Michelle
He said something about within five years for my specific proof set I’ll be looking at about half a million.

Voice
And here’s the crux of the matter. Even though there were literally millions of R5 Mandela coins minted, SA Coin can market them as rare because they say there are only a few of them available in certain high proof or mint state grades. But experts say that does not necessarily make them rare.

Sound Up Glenn
Now there are some of those coins obviously that are top class quality, some of the first coins minted. They would be rare in that condition. But to call a 1994 R5 coin generally rare, taking into account that there were 45 million of them made, is a bit of stretch.

Voice
Despite the fact that none of our case studies have been able to realize any kind of return on their investment, Mark says that many of his investors have made good profits.

Sound Up Mark
Mark: … where you’ve got people that weren’t successful you’ve got a lot of people that were successful.

Claire: We’re struggling to find the people that were successful. I think it would be… Can we get in touch with them, could you put us in contact with those collectors?

Mark: Look, we have got lots of collectors, but they don’t want to be, they don’t want people to know about their sales. But you can see that with the size of this market that it’s impossible that you couldn’t have good secondary market sales.

Voice
Despite our requests, Mark has not provided us with the contact details of a single investor who has seen good returns on his investment in R5 coins. He’s also declined to provide Carte Blanche with the name of the person who supposedly bought one of the coins for R2.5 million. So is the whole Mandela Mania just a farce?

Sound Up Eelco
Claire: Would you recommend the Mandela R5 coin as any type of investment to our viewers?

Eelco: I wouldn’t touch it. Because right now you are going to pay more then it’s ever going to be worth in the long-term future.

Voice
Mark insists the Mandela coins are not a scam – choosing instead to believe that our case studies are suffering from sour grapes.

Sound Up Mark
Essentially we are in a recessionary climate… and it makes people a bit nasty Claire, because they are short of money. And if they are short of money Claire, they will do virtually anything to try and get hold of money.

Voice
But who could blame you for feeling a little peeved at finding out that your R1mil investment, which you’d been promised would double in a few months, was now worth R25 000.

Sound Up Cyprian
You know he’s just totally unconscionable this man.

Voice
We asked Mark about Cyprian’s case

Sound Up Mark
You know he speaks to me on a monthly basis, and I’ve said to him I give you my word, Cyprian, I’ll sell your coins for you, but I cannot sell them if the economic climate is not in the right place.


Sound Up Barry
Claire: Have you been scammed?

Barry: Absolutely. Absolutely. It’s now got to the stage 6 years later it’s not about the value, it’s about the issue. They are continuing to do it on a daily basis, there is no recourse…

Sound Up Michelle
I do feel that I’ve been scammed… Definitely not a good investment to go for

Link
I can’t tell you the true value of the Mandela R5 coins, but experts agree that the dismal track record speaks for itself.

Sound Up Eelco
I think anybody who charged more than a thousand rand for a proof Mandela has probably charged an un-market related rate for that coin.
